blocks.prompt: The Little Board on Wheels
blocks.text: A scooter looks simple, but it is clever. It has two wheels, a deck to stand on, and a handlebar to steer. To go, you put one foot on the deck. You push the ground with your other foot. Each push sends you forward. When you want to turn, you lean and move the handlebar. Most scooters have a brake over the back wheel. You press it with your foot to slow down. A kick scooter needs no fuel and no battery. Your own legs do all the work.

blocks.prompt: One Push, a Long Ride
blocks.text: People have ridden scooters for more than a hundred years. Long ago, children built their own. They nailed a wooden crate to a plank, added roller skate wheels, and pushed off down the street. Those early scooters were heavy and loud. In the 1990s, inventors made a new kind. It was built from light metal, and it folded up small enough to carry in a bag. Around the year 2000, this folding scooter became a craze. Kids all over the world wanted one. A scooter works because of its wheels. Inside each wheel sit tiny metal balls called bearings. The bearings let the wheel spin freely, with almost no rubbing. When you push the ground, you move forward. When you stop pushing, the scooter keeps rolling on its own for a while. That is why one good push can carry you a long way.

blocks.prompt: The Science Hidden in a Kick
blocks.text: Riding a scooter feels easy, but a lot of science is hidden in every push. When you press your foot against the ground, the ground pushes back against you with an equal force. That backward push on the ground becomes a forward push on you. It is the same rule that moves a swimmer through water or a rocket through the sky: push on something, and it pushes you the other way. Once you are moving, a property called momentum takes over. Momentum is the tendency of a moving object to keep moving. Your scooter would roll forever if nothing slowed it down. Something always does. The wheels rub against the ground, the air pushes against your body, and the bearings inside the wheels are not perfectly smooth. Together these forces are called friction, and friction is what forces you to push again and again to keep your speed. Balance is the third piece. A scooter has a narrow deck, so your weight must stay lined up above the wheels. Lean too far to one side and gravity pulls you down. Good riders make tiny corrections without even thinking about it, shifting their weight the way a tightrope walker does. Steering works partly by turning the handlebar and partly by leaning, and skilled riders lean into a turn to carve a smooth curve rather than a sharp, wobbly one.

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Keeps Being Reinvented
blocks.text: Few machines are as simple as a kick scooter, and few have been reinvented as many times. Its ancestor was a homemade toy. In the early twentieth century, city children fastened roller skate wheels to a wooden board and a crate, stood on top, and shoved themselves along the sidewalk. These contraptions were rough and short lived, but they carried the whole idea: a deck to stand on, wheels to roll on, and a handle to steer. The scooter most people picture today arrived much later. In the 1990s, engineers in Europe designed a compact scooter made from aircraft aluminum. It was so light a child could lift it with one hand, and it folded flat enough to slide into a school bag. Around the year 2000 it exploded into a worldwide craze, selling in the millions within months. For a while it seemed like every kid on every street had one. Underneath the fun sits real physics. A scooter turns human effort into motion through a chain of forces. Each kick pushes backward on the ground, and by Newton's third law the ground pushes the rider forward. Ball bearings in the wheels cut friction to almost nothing, so a single strong push glides a surprising distance. Momentum keeps the rider moving between kicks, while friction and air resistance steadily bleed that speed away, which is why the legs never truly get to rest. The story did not stop there. In the 2010s the electric scooter appeared, trading the kicking foot for a small motor and a battery. Rental companies scattered them across city streets by the thousand, and suddenly the scooter was not just a toy but a way for adults to cross a city. The humble board on wheels had grown up, even as the kick scooter it came from stayed exactly as simple, and exactly as useful, as ever.

blocks.prompt: The Honest Machine
blocks.text: A kick scooter is one of the most honest machines a person can ride. There is no engine to hide behind, no fuel gauge, no software. What you put in with your leg is what you get out in speed, and every part of the ride obeys plain, visible physics. That honesty is exactly why the scooter is worth a closer look. Consider how it moves. Motion begins with a push, and that push is governed by Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When the rider's foot presses backward against the pavement, the pavement presses forward against the rider with the same strength. The ground, in effect, throws you ahead. Between kicks, the scooter coasts on momentum, the stored motion of a mass already moving. If the world were frictionless, one push would carry a rider onward without end. It is not, so it does not. Friction lives in three places at once: where the wheels meet the road, where the air meets the rider, and inside the wheel hubs themselves. To fight that last source, engineers pack the wheels with ball bearings, rings of hardened steel spheres that turn sliding contact into rolling contact and shrink the friction to a whisper. The quality of those bearings, more than almost anything else, decides how far a single kick will carry you. Balance is the quieter miracle. A scooter's deck is narrow, so the rider's center of gravity must hover in a thin column above the wheels. Standing still, this is nearly impossible, which is why a stopped scooter tips over. In motion, it becomes easy, because a rolling wheel resists changes to the direction it spins, a property called angular momentum that steadies bicycles and scooters alike. The rider steers with a blend of turning the bar and leaning the body, and the faster the ride, the more the lean does the work. The scooter's history mirrors its mechanics: simple ideas, refined again and again. Early versions were homemade, roller skate wheels bolted to a plank. In the 1990s designers rebuilt the idea in lightweight aluminum, small enough to fold into a bag, and the world bought them by the million. In the 2010s a motor and battery were added, and the electric scooter turned a child's toy into adult transport that now fills city streets. Through every version, the core has not changed. Stand on the deck, hold the bar, push the earth away, and let momentum do the rest. Few machines ask so little and explain so much.
